raw.answer: The case asked whether a tax rule treating imported compressors used to assemble car air conditioners as air conditioners for commodity tax purposes was unconstitutional. The court decided the rule does not conflict with Article 19 of the Constitution, even though its wording does not fully match the commodity tax statute.
raw.held: The 1975 rule that taxes imported compressors for car air conditioners as air conditioners does not conflict with Article 19 of the Constitution.

points.text: The rule's wording does not fully match the commodity tax statute, which taxes electrical devices that adjust temperature, such as air conditioners and heaters.
Such compressors are the main part of an air conditioner and can only be used to assemble car air conditioners, so they still fall within the statute's electrical appliance category.
Car air conditioner parts are spread around the car with no single fixed form, so without taxing the compressor, air conditioners imported in separate pieces would be hard to tax.
No further commodity tax is charged on other parts or on the finished air conditioner, and no new tax item or rate was created, so taxpayers' burden is not increased.
The rule is necessary to simplify tax collection, prevent tax evasion and keep taxation fair.

who: Importers of car air conditioner compressors
Car air conditioner makers and assemblers

raw.answer: The case asked whether a city or provincial council can require a bank to hand over loan data. The court decided that, for state-run banks, a council may require certain overdue loan data in limited circumstances, even though banks are normally bound to keep customer information secret.
raw.held: When a council decides it is needed for reviewing a state-run bank's budget and accounts, the bank must provide data on overdue loans (other than those with no hope of recovery or already reported as bad debts) that appear clearly improper, as long as individual customer names are withheld and the council keeps the data private.

points.text: The banking law's secrecy rule protects customers' financial secrets and stops their dealings with the bank from being freely made public, in order to protect privacy.

The Ministry of Finance's rulings already exempted supervisory, judicial, police and tax authorities' necessary investigations from this secrecy, and allowed legislative bodies limited data in closed sessions, based on banking-business concerns.
State-run banks' budgets and final accounts must by law be reviewed by councils, so councils may need information for that review.

Disclosure is limited to overdue loans, excluding hopeless ones or those reported as bad debts, which are still handled under current rules, and only where there is reasonable ground to think the loan is clearly improper, by council resolution.
Privacy is protected by conditions: the bank does not reveal individual customers' names and the council does not make the data public.
Because of these safeguards, the bank should still provide the data so that the council can supervise state-run banks.

raw.answer: The case was about a Ministry of the Interior rule on surveying urban-plan boundary markers. It said that once a higher-level government had re-surveyed a marker's position, no further objection could be raised. The court held that, to the extent this blocks people from using appeals and administrative lawsuits, it conflicts with Article 16 of the Constitution and must not be applied.
raw.held: The last part of Article 8 of the 1979 urban plan marker survey and management rules, which says no further objection may be raised after a higher-level government's re-survey, restricts people's right to appeal and sue. To that extent it is inconsistent with Article 16 of the Constitution and is not to be applied.

points.text: Article 16 of the Constitution gives people the right to file appeals and lawsuits when their rights are harmed. The bodies that hear them must decide according to law, and an administrative order may not restrict this right.

The urban plan rules let landowners and other interested parties request a re-survey and a further re-survey if they think a marker was placed wrongly. But the last part of Article 8 bars any further objection after the higher-level government's re-survey.

The Administrative Court read 'no further objection' literally as also barring appeals and administrative lawsuits. That limits people's right to seek administrative remedies under the appeal and administrative litigation laws.
Even though the rules provide re-survey remedies, the part that limits appeals and lawsuits is inconsistent with the Constitution's protection of people's rights, so it must not be applied.

who: Landowners and others with rights in affected land
People who dispute a marker's surveyed position

raw.answer: The question was whether, when Taiwan's Control Yuan impeaches a member of the military, the case should go to the Commission on the Discipline of Public Functionaries. The court said yes. It also said that other misconduct by military personnel, outside such impeachments, is still punished under the Army, Navy and Air Force Punishment Act.
raw.held: When the Control Yuan impeaches a military member, it must send the case to the Commission on the Discipline of Public Functionaries for review. Other offenses by military personnel are still punished under the Army, Navy and Air Force Punishment Act.

points.text: The Judicial Yuan is the highest judicial organ and handles discipline of public officials, and its Commission on the Discipline of Public Functionaries is the body in charge of that discipline.

The Constitution gives the Control Yuan a broad impeachment power. Apart from the President and Vice President, it does not treat civilian and military officials differently when impeachment cases are reviewed.

So an impeachment of a military member must be sent with its evidence to the Commission on the Discipline of Public Functionaries, in line with Article 77 of the Constitution. The Control Yuan Act and the Public Functionaries Discipline Act were written on this basis.

For active-duty military misconduct that is not criminal and is not an impeachment, punishment stays under the Army, Navy and Air Force Punishment Act. This keeps military command and the power to reward and punish united and ensures commands are carried out.

who: Commission on the Discipline of Public Functionaries

raw.answer: The case asked whether a traffic law is unconstitutional when it revokes the driver's license of a driver who causes injury or death and then flees. The court decided the rule does not conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: Article 62, paragraph 2 of the Road Traffic Management and Penalty Act requires a driver who causes injury or death to give aid or take other necessary steps, report to the police, and not flee, on pain of license revocation. The court held this is permitted under Article 23 of the Constitution and does not conflict with it.

points.text: After an accident with injury or death, aid or necessary measures should be taken promptly to keep the harm from growing.
Fleeing the scene makes it hard to determine responsibility and may cost an injured person their life, so strict treatment is needed.
The rule aims to improve driving safety, protect others' rights and maintain social order, which Article 23 of the Constitution permits.
Whether a driver left without knowing they had caused an accident is a question of facts and law application in individual cases, and is outside this interpretation.

who: Drivers who cause accidents with injury or death

raw.answer: The case asked whether the central government, or the existing provincial representative bodies, could on their own pass laws setting up a specific provincial assembly and provincial government. The court decided that under the Constitution's rules on local government, neither can do so. It also said existing rules on Taiwan Province's local self-government and its assembly and government stay valid for now.
raw.held: The central government has no constitutional basis to make a law alone on the organization of a specific provincial assembly and provincial government, and the provincial representative bodies now in place have no power to legislate on it themselves.

points.text: The request was about how the Constitution divides legislative power over local self-government, not about whether a law is unconstitutional.

Articles 108, 112 and 113 of the Constitution set special rules on dividing legislative power over provincial and county self-government. Under them, the center cannot alone legislate on a specific provincial assembly and government, and current provincial bodies cannot legislate on it themselves.

Unforeseen developments since the Constitution took effect should be handled by the central government, weighing national needs and local conditions, through a solution that follows constitutional procedure.

Until then provincial and county self-government and administration cannot be interrupted. For the same reason as Interpretation No. 259, the current rules on Taiwan Province's self-government and its assembly and government remain valid.

who: Provincial assembly and provincial government of Taiwan

raw.answer: The case asked whether handling fines for tax-law violations through administrative orders rather than statutes is unconstitutional. The court held that where tax laws let courts set fines by ruling, the procedure for handling them must be set by law to protect people's rights. The older interpretations and the 1972 Executive Yuan rules were stopgaps and will lose effect within two years.
raw.held: The procedure for court-ordered tax fines must be set by law. Two earlier interpretations (Nos. 3685 and 4006) and the Executive Yuan's 1972 revised financial case handling rules lose effect from this ruling's announcement, at the latest when two years have passed.

points.text: Fines for tax violations are administrative penalties, but tax laws may, as a policy choice, have courts decide them by ruling.

Such fine cases are neither civil nor criminal cases. Before the Court Organization Act was amended, ordinary courts had only those two kinds, so these cases were handled under criminal procedure using Executive Yuan rules.
That arrangement was an unavoidable stopgap while the legal system was incomplete and should not last long.
So the penalty and remedy procedures for these fines must be set by law, in line with the constitution's protection of people's rights.

Because making laws takes time, the old interpretations (no new-evidence correction after a final fine ruling; no remedy for erroneous appeal rulings) and the 1972 rules end within two years at the latest.

In the meantime the responsible authorities should review and revise the relevant laws, recognizing that civil, criminal and administrative procedures differ, and considering reform of administrative litigation and enforcement.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a tax rule was unconstitutional that made a person penalized under the Commodity Tax Act pay the fine or put up a guarantee before being allowed to appeal. The court decided that the rule, in the version before the January 24, 1990 amendment, unnecessarily limited people's right to go to court and conflicted with Article 16 of the Constitution.
raw.held: Paragraph 3 of Article 20 of the Commodity Tax Act (version before the January 24, 1990 amendment) took away the chance to appeal from people who could not pay the fine or provide a deposit or guarantor. This was an unnecessary limit on the right to sue and conflicts with Article 16 of the Constitution.

points.text: The right to sue protected by Article 16 includes the right to appeal against a lower court's decision, and it may be restricted only where Article 23 says it is necessary.

Under the old Act, penalties and confiscation were referred by the tax office to a court for a ruling, and the person could appeal within ten days, but the third paragraph required a deposit of the fine or the goods' value, or a reliable guarantor, first.
The rule was meant to stop people from appealing casually to delay paying the fine, but an appeal does not stop enforcement.
So people who could not meet the requirement lost any chance to appeal, an unnecessary limit on the right to sue that conflicts with Article 16.

who: People penalized under the old Commodity Tax Act
People unable to pay a deposit or find a guarantor

raw.answer: The case asked whether two Executive Yuan rules were unconstitutional: one left funeral subsidies for public employees' family members out of retirement pay, and the other let only serving staff, not retirees, claim that subsidy. The court decided both rules are consistent with the Constitution.
raw.held: The Executive Yuan's 1980 letter, which left the funeral subsidy out of retirement pay, is consistent with the legislative purpose of the retirement regulations. The living-allowance guidelines, which retirees cannot use to claim the subsidy, do not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: The retirement regulations define monthly salary as actual base pay plus other cash payments. A funeral subsidy is not paid monthly but only when a particular event occurs, so it cannot be part of monthly salary.
So leaving the subsidy out of retirement pay does not go against the purpose of the retirement regulations.
The living-allowance guidelines were made to stabilize the livelihood of public employees, and are a discretionary measure by the responsible authority.
The guidelines apply only to serving staff within an agency's budgeted headcount, so retirees cannot claim the funeral subsidy under them.

The authorities may give retirees extra help beyond legal retirement benefits, weighing national finances and the nature of each allowance. This is within administrative discretion, and not every allowance must match what serving staff get.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a provision of the Fiscal Revenue and Expenditure Allocation Act is unconstitutional. It says the central government makes general rules for taxes (tax law general principles) that provinces and counties then rely on when making their own tax laws. The court held that the provision does not conflict with the Constitution, and it told the central government to make those general rules quickly.
raw.held: The latter part of Article 7 of the Fiscal Revenue and Expenditure Allocation Act, under which the central government sets general tax rules as the basis for provincial and county tax legislation, does not conflict with the Constitution. The central government should promptly make or add the general rules, and until localities legislate, the relevant central tax laws still apply.

points.text: The provision serves the central government's constitutional power to divide national taxes from provincial and county taxes, and it upholds the principle that taxes must rest on law.
The Constitution's grant of provincial and county tax legislation means localities may make and carry out their own laws on taxes already assigned to them under a reasonable central division.
So the central government should make local tax general rules, or put general provisions usable by localities into each tax law, so localities can use their constitutional legislative power.
No such general rules exist now and some current tax laws lack them, so they should be made or added promptly.
Until localities finish legislating, the central tax laws on local taxes stay in effect and must be followed.
The central government should adjust the revenue division in good time, considering actual conditions, to keep central and local finances balanced as the Constitution intends.

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Cooperative Act and related rules are unconstitutional because they do not clearly set out the conditions and procedure for dissolving a cooperative. The court said the dissolution order under the Act is a measure that ends a cooperative's legal personality, and the Act does not clearly state its conditions and procedure. It said the authorities should review and amend the law, and the related incentive rules should be reviewed along with it. The ruling does not say in these paragraphs that anything was declared unconstitutional.
raw.held: The Cooperative Act's dissolution order is a measure dissolving a cooperative, and the Act lacks clear conditions and procedure, so the competent authority should review and amend it. The Interior Ministry's 1980 rule letting local authorities order dissolution of cooperatives graded 戊 should be reviewed and amended along with the law.

points.text: Article 55(1)(6) of the Cooperative Act lists a dissolution order as a ground for dissolving a cooperative, and this order is a measure that ends the cooperative's legal personality.
The Act does not clearly set out the conditions and procedure for such a measure, so the competent authority should review and amend it.
The Interior Ministry's 1980 incentive rule, under which cooperatives graded 戊 are ordered dissolved by local authorities, has a legitimate purpose.
Because the Act itself is to be reviewed and amended, that rule should also be reviewed and amended together with it.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Supreme Court precedent was constitutional. The precedent said that when a court wrongly rejected a valid appeal against a defendant on procedural grounds, that judgment had no real binding effect and the court could go straight to judging the case on its merits. The court held that this is inconsistent with the constitution's guarantee of due legal process, so the precedent should no longer be applied within the scope of this ruling.
raw.held: When a valid appeal that goes against the defendant is wrongly dismissed as invalid and that judgment becomes final, it is a serious legal error, but the judgment must first be set aside through the extraordinary appeal procedure before the original proceedings can resume. Otherwise it conflicts with Article 8, paragraph 1 of the Constitution, and the 1936 Supreme Court precedent is no longer to be applied within this scope.

points.text: Article 8(1) of the Constitution says people may not be tried or punished except through legal procedure, and the Code of Criminal Procedure likewise says no one may be prosecuted or punished except through the procedures it sets out.

A criminal case ended by a final judgment, whether on the merits or on procedure, is legally binding. Under the cited earlier interpretations, a procedural dismissal of a valid appeal against the defendant cannot be reopened and judged on the merits until it has been set aside through legal procedure.

Criminal procedure must protect the parties' right to bring valid proceedings, while also taking into account the defendant's reliance on a judgment's effect and the correct exercise of the state's power to punish.

Because the wrongful dismissal still has the form of a judgment, it can lead the defendant to rely on its binding effect, so it must first be revoked by extraordinary appeal. Skipping this conflicts with Article 8(1), and the precedent that allowed it is no longer to be applied within this scope.

who: Criminal defendants whose valid appeals were wrongly dismissed

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Police Offense Punishment Act (違警罰法) is unconstitutional because it lets police authorities restrict people's personal freedom. The court decided that having police authorities decide detention, labor penalties, and the Article 28 'sending to a suitable place for correction or training in living skills' measures does not fit Article 8, paragraph 1 of the Constitution. These decisions must be moved to the courts, following legal procedures.
raw.held: Police-issued rulings on detention, labor penalties, and the Article 28 correction or skills-training measures must be handed to the courts under legal procedures. The old police-decision rules lose effect no later than July 1, 1991, and the related laws must be revised before then; Interpretation No. 166 is supplemented.

points.text: Article 8, paragraph 1 of the Constitution protects personal freedom: arrest or detention must follow legal procedure by judicial or police bodies, and only a court may try and punish by legal procedure.
Detention and labor penalties decided by police authorities punish people's bodily freedom, so Interpretation No. 166 had already said they should promptly be moved to the courts.
The Article 28 measure of sending someone to a suitable place for correction or learning living skills is attached to the offense penalty and likewise restricts personal freedom.

For the same reason as in Interpretation No. 166, police authorities deciding this measure directly does not fit Article 8, paragraph 1, so it must go to the courts together with detention and labor penalties.
The affected procedural rules lose effect by July 1, 1991 at the latest, and the laws must be revised before then.

who: People subject to police offense penalties
People sent to correction or skills training under Article 28

raw.answer: The case asked whether members of the first-term central representative bodies, who kept serving after a national crisis prevented new elections, could serve without any term limit. The court said their continued service was needed to keep the constitutional system running, but it was never meant to be unlimited. Those who were never re-elected must stop serving by 31 December 1991, and the government must hold new national elections.
raw.held: First-term central representatives who were never re-elected must end their service by 31 December 1991. Those who in practice cannot serve or regularly do not serve must be identified and removed immediately, and the government must hold the next national elections in good time.

points.text: The Constitution sets fixed terms for central representatives: 6 years for National Assembly delegates, 3 years for legislators and 6 years for control members.

After the national crisis, elections could not be held, so the earlier interpretation (No. 31) let first-term legislators and control members keep serving to avoid halting the five-branch system, and National Assembly delegates kept serving under the Constitution's Article 28, paragraph 2.
Regular elections reflect public opinion and carry out constitutional democracy, and continued service was only a response to the situation at the time.
Interpretation No. 31, Article 28 and the Temporary Provisions were never meant to allow unlimited service, to change terms, or to limit later elections.
Since 1969 the government has held elections for central representatives in the free area, gradually filling the central bodies, so those not re-elected should end service by the stated date.

Constitutional election provisions still cannot fully apply in practice, so the government must plan next elections, including nationwide at-large seats, to keep the system working; added-seat members serve until their terms end.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Supreme Court precedent on who counts as a "victim of a crime" entitled to bring a private prosecution is unconstitutional. The court decided the precedent is not clearly in conflict with the Constitution. It also said the range of victims who may bring private prosecutions should be reviewed and clearly set out.
raw.held: The legal view in the Supreme Court's 1981 precedent (70 Tai-shang 1799) is hard to see as conflicting with the Constitution, because the law does not define "victim" and the trial court may decide it on the facts of each case.

points.text: The Constitution protects the right to bring lawsuits, but how a case proceeds is to be set by law, as an earlier interpretation (No. 170) explained.
Criminal procedure sets up public prosecution by prosecutors, and victims can file a complaint with a prosecutor to have the case investigated and prosecuted.

The private prosecution article lets a "victim of a crime" prosecute, meaning the direct victim, but the law does not clearly define who that is in crimes harming the state or society as well as individuals.
So the trial court may decide, on the specific facts of each case, who is a direct victim.
Where private prosecution cannot be used, public prosecution still applies, so state punishment is not hindered and the right to sue is not restricted.

The precedent held that in a public official profit-seeking offense the direct harm is to the state, so a private person harmed only indirectly cannot bring a private prosecution; this was not clearly unconstitutional, though the scope should be reviewed and clearly set out.

raw.answer: The Taipei City Council asked the court to clarify what "provincial (municipal) government" means in Article 15 of the Labor Insurance Act, which says those governments subsidize labor insurance premiums. The court decided the term means any province or city that has workers insured under certain categories, whether or not it has set up its own labor insurance bureau.
raw.held: "Provincial (municipal) government" in Article 15 means the province or city that has workers insured under the categories in items 2 to 4 of the same article. It does not depend on whether that government directly set up a labor insurance bureau.

points.text: The Taipei City Council, while reviewing the city government's budget, said the city's subsidy budget, based on the Council of Labor Affairs' view, conflicted with Article 5 of the Act, and asked for a uniform interpretation. The court said the request should be accepted.

The premium subsidy of 20% or 40% is meant to ease the premium burden of workers in the area: those without a fixed employer or who are self-employed and join occupational unions or fishermen's associations, outsourced seamen in seamen's unions or captains' associations, and laid-off staff who voluntarily continue insurance. This protects workers' livelihoods and promotes social security, and it is a duty of provincial (municipal) governments in labor welfare.
So "provincial (municipal) government" means the province or city that has such workers insured as members.

Article 5, which lets governments in areas with many workers set up labor insurance bureaus before a central bureau exists, was made to fit practical circumstances and is unrelated to who must pay the subsidy.

who: Workers insured through occupational unions or fishermen's associations
Outsourced seamen in seamen's unions or captains' associations
Laid-off workers who continue insurance voluntarily

raw.answer: The case asked which judges must step aside (recuse themselves) when a party files a retrial case against a final judgment. The court decided that judges who took part in the final judgment under challenge must also step aside in the retrial, but only once. It also said a Supreme Court precedent that conflicts with this should no longer be applied.
raw.held: Judges who took part in a final judgment must recuse themselves from a retrial case challenging it, but the recusal is limited to one time. The conflicting part of Supreme Court precedent No. 362 (year 26) is no longer to be applied.

points.text: The Constitution gives people the right to bring lawsuits, which is meant to secure fair trials under lawful procedures.

The Civil Procedure Code's recusal rule keeps a judge from acting in the appeal or remedy stage of a decision they took part in, so the judge stays objective and the benefit of court levels and fairness of judgments are protected.
By the same reasoning, judges who took part in the final judgment being challenged must also step aside in the retrial proceeding.

Because courts have a limited number of judges and retrial suits have no limit on how many can be filed, recusal is limited to one time, following the spirit of the Administrative Litigation Act's rule.

For example, if a retrial is sought against both a retrial final judgment and the original final judgment, only judges in the retrial final judgment must step aside, not those in the original judgment.

The old Supreme Court precedent said the judgment challenged in a retrial is not a prior decision, so no recusal was needed. To the extent it conflicts with this ruling, it is no longer applied, to protect the right to a fair trial.

who: Judges who took part in a final judgment

raw.answer: The case asked whether a person who was pardoned, and who might be able to return to a public office lost through a criminal conviction, can ask to have that office restored. The court said a pardon that declares a conviction and sentence void does not undo sentences already carried out, but it does restore lost civil rights from the day the pardon takes effect. For public offices lost through the conviction, the person may apply to the responsible authority, which handles the request under the relevant laws, if the office can be restored going forward.
raw.held: A presidential pardon that voids a conviction and sentence has no retroactive effect on sentences already served. Any deprivation of public rights ends from the day the pardon takes effect, and a person who lost a public office may apply to the responsible authority if it can be restored going forward.

points.text: The Constitution (Article 40) gives the President the power to grant amnesty, pardon, sentence reduction and restoration of rights, and the Pardon Act (Article 3) allows a pardon to declare a conviction and sentence void in special circumstances.
To keep the legal order stable and respect effects that already arose from lawful enforcement, such a pardon does not reach back to sentences already carried out.
Because the conviction and sentence become void from the day the pardon takes effect, a deprivation of public rights ends from that same day and those rights are restored.

A public office lost through a final guilty judgment, if it can be restored going forward, may be dealt with by the responsible authority on the person's application, under this interpretation and relevant laws.

who: People who received a pardon voiding their conviction
People deprived of public rights by a conviction
People who lost public office through a final conviction

raw.answer: The case asked whether an accountant who objects to a final decision of the Ministry of Finance's accountant disciplinary review committee can take it to administrative court. The court decided that this review decision is in effect the final appeal decision, so no further appeal steps are needed. An accountant who believes the decision is unlawful and harms their rights may go directly to administrative court.
raw.held: The review committee's decision on disciplining an accountant is substantively equal to a final appeal decision, so no further petition or second petition is allowed or needed. The disciplined person may sue directly in administrative court if they think the decision is unlawful and harms their rights.

points.text: The constitutional right to petition against administrative actions exists so the agency or its superior can correct unlawful or improper actions; if another legal remedy already achieves this, it is substantively equal to an appeal and no further appeal step is needed.

The appeals law's proviso ("unless the law provides otherwise") covers this situation, and it does not mean a person who has used up an equivalent remedy is barred from going on to administrative court.
The disciplinary committee's decision to discipline an accountant is an administrative action, and asking for a review of it is substantively like an appeal.

So the review committee's decision equals a final appeal decision, with no need for another petition or second petition; the disciplined person may go directly to administrative court, in line with Article 16 of the Constitution protecting the right to sue.

who: Ministry of Finance accountant disciplinary committees

raw.answer: The case asked whether special municipalities (directly governed cities) must set aside the same share of their budgets for education, science and culture as provinces do. The court decided that they must, because a special municipality has a constitutional status comparable to a province. Its share is therefore set by the rule for provinces, not the rule for ordinary cities and counties.
raw.held: Article 164's minimum shares set the portion of total annual expenditure that each level of government must devote to education, science and culture. A special municipality's share is to follow the rule for provinces.

points.text: Article 164 sets minimum shares of the budget for education, science and culture: 15% for the central government, 25% for provinces, and 35% for cities and counties. The 'budget total' means the total expenditure in the annual general budget for ordinary governance, as earlier interpretations Nos. 77 and 231 explained.
The word 'city' in the Constitution sometimes means only provincial cities and sometimes also includes special municipalities, so the word alone does not settle the question.

Because Article 118 places self-governance of special municipalities within the chapter section on provinces, a special municipality that practices self-governance is a local self-governing body at the same level as a province, with comparable status, powers, responsibilities, finances and burdens.

Special municipalities are densely populated and unusual in political, economic and cultural terms, and their infrastructure needs cost more than those of counties and provincial cities. Their finances must be allocated carefully so that city development stays balanced.
So a special municipality's share of the budget for education, science and culture should follow the provincial rule.

who: Residents who rely on education, science and culture spending

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule set under the Ministry of Economic Affairs, which lets state-run enterprises set earlier retirement ages by job grade, violates the Constitution. The court decided it does not, because until a law on the hiring and retirement of public enterprise employees exists, the rule serves to renew staff and run the enterprises on business lines. The court also said such a law should be made quickly.
raw.held: The provision allowing grade-based, age-limited early retirement standards for the Ministry's enterprise employees does not conflict with the Constitution before the relevant law is made. The hiring and retirement of public enterprise employees affect their rights and duties, so a law should be made promptly.

points.text: The Constitution does not say whether hiring and retirement of public enterprise employees must follow the civil servant laws, so the legislature may set this by law within the spirit of the Constitution.

Under the civil servant retirement law, its enforcement rules and the civil servant appointment law's provision that public enterprise staff appointments be set by separate law, public enterprise employees cannot retire under the civil servant retirement law until that law exists.

The Labor Standards Act's reference to applying civil servant rules does not make the civil servant appointment or retirement laws apply directly before the separate laws exist, nor displace existing rules.

The Ministry's retirement measure lets enterprises set earlier retirement standards by job nature, with minimum ages of 55 for staff and 50 for workers. Before the laws exist, it serves staff renewal and business-style management, so it is not unconstitutional.
Because these matters affect employees' rights and duties, a law should still be made quickly.

who: Employees of Ministry of Economic Affairs state enterprises

raw.answer: The case asked whether members of the National Assembly are unpaid positions. The court decided that they are, because the Assembly does not meet regularly. Any payment they receive in special situations, such as when the Assembly meets, must be set out in a law, and all members in the same period must get the same pay.
raw.held: National Assembly representatives hold unpaid posts and are not owed regular salaries or public allowances. Any pay for special situations, such as when the Assembly meets, must have its items and standards set by law before it can be budgeted, and the pay must be the same for all representatives in the same period. Representatives added under the Temporary Provisions receive the same pay as Second National Assembly representatives. The ruling takes effect on 1 January 1992 (ROC year 81).

points.text: The duties of Assembly representatives under the Constitution do not involve regular meetings, and representatives are not barred from holding other public posts or doing other work, so the job does not call for regular state-paid salaries and is unpaid.

Interpretation No. 76 said the National Assembly, Legislative Yuan and Control Yuan together are comparable to a parliament, but this does not mean they have the same nature, powers or staff pay. That earlier interpretation is supplemented.

Pay received in special situations, such as when the Assembly meets, and the pay of other central representatives affect taxpayers' burden, so the items and standards must be set by law before budget money can be paid.

Under the principle of equality, representatives must receive the same pay in the same period, and those added under the Temporary Provisions receive the same as the Second National Assembly representatives.
Making or amending the relevant laws takes time, so the ruling takes effect on 1 January 1992 (ROC year 81).

who: Representatives added under the Temporary Provisions

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Equalization of Land Rights Act and its enforcement rules, which tax the rise in land value, violate the Constitution. The court decided they do not conflict with Article 15 or Article 143, paragraph 3 of the Constitution. It reasoned that the tax is meant to return natural land value gains to the public, and that the owner's improvement costs are deducted.
raw.held: The provisions of the Equalization of Land Rights Act (Articles 35 and 36, paragraphs 1 and 2) and Article 53 of its enforcement rules, which levy a land value increment tax on natural gains after deducting improvement costs, do not conflict with Constitution Articles 15 and 143, paragraph 3.

points.text: Article 143, paragraph 3 of the Constitution aims to carry out the policy of returning natural land value gains to the public.
Under the Act and rules, the tax is calculated on the total rise in land value minus all the money the owner already spent improving the land.
Any value added by improvements is hard to identify and calculate, so it cannot be clearly separated from the natural gain.
The tax does not take the whole rise in value, which is enough to take the owner's interests into account.

The court noted that how to set standards for deducting improvement costs, whether stricter or looser, is linked to tax rates and whether income tax is also levied. It said the relevant authorities should review this over time within the legislature's discretion.

who: Landowners who declared land value and face the tax
Authorities that set and collect the tax
Legislators and agencies reviewing deduction standards

raw.answer: The case concerned what kind of appeal civil servants must have when they are disciplined, especially when the discipline changes their status or seriously affects them. The court said a superior may impose discipline under a law, within reasonable limits. But a person given a status-changing or seriously affecting punishment may challenge it before the judicial body in charge of discipline, which reviews whether it was unlawful or improper.
raw.held: Discipline that can change a civil servant's status or seriously affects them may be challenged before the judicial body that handles discipline, which reviews whether the original decision was unlawful or improper. The related laws must be amended accordingly, and Interpretation No. 243 is supplemented.

points.text: Article 77 makes the Judicial Yuan the highest body for disciplining civil servants, but this does not mean every disciplinary act must be carried out directly by it.

Discipline is the state's sanction for unlawful or neglectful conduct and is needed to maintain a superior's supervisory power, so the law may let superiors impose it within reasonable limits depending on its nature.

For discipline that can change status or seriously affect a civil servant, the person may object to the judicial body in charge of discipline, which reviews whether the decision was unlawful or improper.
The laws on civil servant discipline and performance evaluation must be amended in line with this, and Interpretation No. 243 is supplemented.
Under No. 243, dismissed civil servants may bring administrative litigation only until the laws are amended, when they may seek judicial relief.
A qualified, status-protected civil servant removed from their post by a non-disciplinary measure, who got no relief through administrative procedures, may still sue under No. 243.

who: Civil servants dismissed or removed from post

raw.answer: The Legislative Yuan and the National Assembly were unsure what Interpretation No. 282 meant by National Assembly delegates being 'unsalaried' and able to receive pay 'in specific circumstances', so they asked the court to clarify. The court explained that 'unsalaried' means delegates should not receive regular, fixed stipends or equivalents from the national treasury, not that they can never be paid anything. Reasonable payments when the Assembly meets to exercise its powers are allowed, and the legislature must set the items and standards by law.
raw.held: 'Unsalaried' means delegates are not to get regular fixed stipends or similar payments from the treasury, but it does not mean no pay at all. Pay for convening to exercise powers is allowed, and the legislature must set suitable items and standards by law, including necessary expenses within reasonable limits; the same applies when revising pay laws for other central representatives.

points.text: The request was accepted because the Legislative Yuan and National Assembly, in applying Interpretation No. 282, had doubts about its wording, and that interpretation concerns only central representatives' pay.
Pay of central representatives, whatever it is called, burdens taxpayers and is an important state matter, so suitable items and standards must first be set by law before a budget can pay them.
National Assembly delegates' pay had no legal basis, and the older law for other central representatives did not match actual payments, so both needed review to build a system of lawful pay.

'Unsalaried' means no regular fixed payment from the treasury of stipends or equivalents, not no remuneration in every case; reasonable pay when meeting to exercise powers is the main example of permitted pay.

Which other circumstances allow pay is for the legislature to decide, including necessary costs directly tied to exercising powers (such as postal, telecom and transport costs) and insurance subsidies during the term, within reasonable limits.

Delegates added under the Temporary Provisions who sat with second-term delegates from 1 January 1992 should receive pay consistent with the second-term delegates, based on public interest and equality.

who: Delegates added under the Temporary Provisions

raw.answer: The case asked whether a court precedent that barred public servants from challenging decisions affecting their property rights was unconstitutional. The court said public servants who are dismissed under the civil service performance appraisal law may bring an administrative lawsuit, but other appraisal results that leave their status unchanged still cannot be challenged that way. It also said a public servant whose property claim, based on a final appraisal result, is refused may file an administrative appeal or lawsuit, and the old precedent no longer applies to the extent it conflicts.
raw.held: A dismissal under the performance appraisal law can be challenged in an administrative lawsuit, but other appraisal results that do not change status cannot. A public servant whose property claim based on a final appraisal result is refused may seek an administrative appeal or lawsuit, and the 1959 Administrative Court precedent (No. 11) is no longer to be applied where it conflicts with this.

points.text: Whether a public servant can sue over an administrative decision depends on what the decision does, in keeping with the constitutional protection of people's rights.
A dismissal changes the person's status and directly affects the constitutional right to hold public office, so the dismissed public servant may bring an administrative lawsuit.
Appraisal results that do not change status still cannot be challenged through an administrative lawsuit.
Refusal of a property claim based on a final appraisal result affects the property right, so an administrative appeal or lawsuit is not ruled out.

The 1959 precedent treated disputes within a special power relationship or private-law employment as barred from appeal, and to the extent it conflicts with this reasoning it is no longer to be applied.
Whether a claim is truly based on a final appraisal result is a question of fact to be decided case by case and is outside this interpretation.

who: Public servants dismissed under the performance appraisal law
Public servants refused property claims based on final appraisal results
Public servants with other appraisal results that don't change status

raw.answer: The case asked whether a serving military officer may move to a civilian government job through "outside-post suspension of service" without breaking the constitutional rule that active-duty soldiers cannot hold civil office. The court decided this is not unconstitutional, because the officer is no longer an active-duty soldier once service is suspended. It also said the current arrangements should be thoroughly reviewed and set directly by law.
raw.held: Moving an officer who has the legal qualifications for a civil post, and who is under retirement age, into a civilian job suited to their expertise through outside-post suspension of service is not shown to conflict with the Constitution. The current practices should be reviewed and set directly by law.

points.text: Article 140 bars only soldiers currently serving from holding civil office at the same time, to prevent soldiers from meddling in politics and to protect normal democratic government.
Soldiers who have retired, been discharged or had service suspended and serve in the reserves have no military power, so there is no risk of political interference.

Under the cited service rules, an officer approved for a public post outside the military has service suspended, enters the reserves, and is placed under reserve management, so they are a reserve soldier and no longer in active service.
Such a move to a suitable civilian job differs from an active-duty soldier holding civil office, so it is hard to call it contrary to the Constitution.
The current rules only provide for "suspension of service" and do not directly provide for "outside-post suspension," which appears only in the implementing rules.

Because those who move to civilian posts can return to active service or be promoted in rank, there is a worry that military and civil roles blur. When such a move is allowed and how return works concern personnel systems, so they should be reviewed and set by law.

who: Active-duty military officers moving to civilian posts

raw.answer: The case asked whether a government guideline on managing publications was unconstitutional. The guideline lets a city's publication enforcement group use work inspection cards. The court held that giving the cards to staff of the city government's own agencies is constitutional, but giving them to people outside those agencies is inconsistent with the ruling and may no longer be applied.
raw.held: Issuing inspection cards to members of the city's enforcement group from city government agencies does not violate the Constitution, because the cards only identify the holders. Issuing cards to people not belonging to city government agencies does not fit this ruling and may no longer be applied.

points.text: Under the Publication Law, the authorities may issue warnings and fines, ban sale or distribution, seize publications, suspend publication for a period, or revoke registration when a publication breaks the law.
Because publication content covers a very wide range of matters, the Government Information Office issued the 1987 guideline to carry out these legal rules.

The guideline sets up a coordination and enforcement group in each directly governed city, led by the city's information office head, with members from the city's information, police, education and social affairs agencies, who carry the inspection cards.
The card only identifies the holder when doing publication work. It does not allow any inspection the law does not permit.
So this part of the guideline stays within the scope of enforcement procedure and does not conflict with the Constitution.

Issuing cards to people outside the city government's agencies is inconsistent with this reasoning and may no longer be applied. The ruling covers only the issuing of inspection cards, not other matters of publication management.

who: City government staff enforcing publication rules
People outside city government agencies who were given inspection cards

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in the National Security Act of the mobilization period was unconstitutional. The rule bars appeals to ordinary courts in finalized military trials of civilians held during martial law, once martial law ends. The court ruled the rule does not conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: The rule barring appeals or complaints to ordinary courts in finalized martial-law military trials of non-military civilians is not unconstitutional. Retrial or extraordinary appeal remains available where legal grounds exist, and the ruling applies only to this particular martial law period.

points.text: The Constitution says civilians are not tried by military courts except active-duty soldiers, but martial law is an exception the Constitution recognizes, as reflected in Articles 8 and 9 of the Martial Law Act.
The Martial Law Act lets such cases be appealed to ordinary courts after martial law ends, which fits the Constitution's intent.
This martial law lasted over thirty years, from 1949 in Taiwan until 1987, which is a very special situation.
With so much time passed, gathering evidence is hard, so barring appeals in finalized cases secures the stability of judgments and is needed to maintain social order.
People with grounds for retrial or extraordinary appeal can still apply for them, so rights are adequately protected and there is no conflict with the Constitution.
Martial law periods that are not this special situation are not covered by this interpretation.

who: Civilians tried by military courts during martial law

raw.answer: The case asked whether the election and recall law's limits on the education and work experience of candidates for representative bodies at every level violate the Constitution. The court held the limits do not conflict with the Constitution. It also said they should be reviewed as education spreads, and that if kept they should be meaningful and take account of people who have real difficulty attending school.
raw.held: The education and experience limits on candidates for representative bodies in Article 32, paragraph 1 of the 1989 amended election and recall law do not conflict with the Constitution. The legislature should review them and, if it keeps them, make suitable provision for people with real difficulty getting schooling.

points.text: Article 130 of the Constitution sets ages for voting and standing for election, and the law may set reasonable conditions on how the right to stand is exercised.

The limits differ from those in other countries, but they aim to improve the work and quality of representative bodies and, given national conditions, cannot be said to conflict with the Constitution.

Because education is becoming more widespread and voters are better able to choose candidates, the limits should be reviewed from time to time, with reference to the common practice of other democracies.

If the limits are kept, their real meaning should matter, and the legislature should use reasonable discretion to make suitable rules for people with real difficulty getting schooling, for example because of a physical or other obstacle.

The court accepted the case even though the law on state compensation does not say whether the legality of an administrative act must first go through administrative litigation, because the case had already ended in a final civil judgment.

who: Candidates for representative bodies at all levels
People who have real difficulty getting schooling

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule made by the Examination Yuan could stop some civil service exam passers from also getting professional and technical qualification at the same time. The court held that the rule added a restriction the law did not contain, and so it should not be applied.
raw.held: The enforcement rule requiring civil service exam passers to also reach the professional exam's pass standard conflicts with the Examination Law and with the constitutional protection of people's rights. Under Article 172 of the Constitution, it must not be applied.

points.text: The Constitution gives people the right to take exams and hold public office. Passing exams is the necessary route to civil service or professional qualifications, which affect people's right to work, so these qualifications are protected and cannot simply be restricted by an order.

Article 7 of the Examination Law, as amended in 1962, gives both qualifications at once when eligibility and exam subjects are the same, which was meant to spare candidates from sitting separate exams.
The law does not require the two exams to have the same pass standard, so when the standards differ it is hard to deny a civil service passer the professional qualification too.
If the law was thought incomplete, it should have been amended first. The Examination Yuan proposed an amendment, but the Legislative Yuan voted in 1980 to keep Article 7 unchanged.

The 1982 enforcement rule added a restriction the law lacks, so some civil service passers could not get both qualifications. This conflicts with the law and with the protection of people's rights, so under Article 172 it is not to be applied.

raw.answer: The case asked whether it is unconstitutional for the self-government of special municipalities (直轄市) to rest on administrative orders. The court noted that the Constitution says a law should set this out, but no such law has been made, so the current system runs on rules issued by the central government. It said such a law should be made, and that the existing central rules stay valid until then.
raw.held: A law on self-government of special municipalities should be made, taking current conditions into account. Until it exists, the current rules issued by the central government remain in effect.

points.text: Article 118 of the Constitution says special municipality self-government is to be set by law, and the Constitution treats provinces, counties and special municipalities differently, so a law must be made even though the procedure need not match that for provinces and counties.
No such law has been made; the organization of special municipalities and their self-government matters currently follow rules issued by the central government.
To carry out the Constitution's intent on local self-government, a law should be made promptly in light of present conditions.
Self-government and local administration cannot be interrupted, so the existing central rules continue to be valid until the law is made.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Finance letter was unconstitutional for saying that money from a court-ordered auction of property is taxed as income from a property transaction. The court decided the letter does not go beyond the Income Tax Act and does not conflict with Article 19 of the Constitution.
raw.held: When a court auctions property under the Compulsory Execution Act, the sale price, after deducting cost and expenses, is counted as property transaction income and taxed together with other income. The Ministry's 1977 letter saying so does not exceed the Income Tax Act and does not conflict with Article 19 of the Constitution.

points.text: Article 19 of the Constitution says people have a duty to pay tax according to law.
Under the Income Tax Act, individuals with income from Taiwan sources pay comprehensive income tax, and income from trading property and rights is counted in that total.

If a court auction of a debtor's property brings in more than the original cost plus the expenses of acquiring, improving and transferring it, the remainder is still property transaction income, so it is included in the debtor's total income and taxed.

The Ministry's letter says a court-auctioned house is still taxed on the auction price minus cost and expenses, together with other income. This stays within the Income Tax Act and does not conflict with Article 19.

who: Debtors whose property is sold at court auction

raw.answer: The case asked whether a earlier court precedent was unconstitutional for saying state-run enterprises cannot be sued as defendants in administrative lawsuits. The court held that a group set up by law, which the government has legally given public authority over particular matters, can be a defendant in an administrative suit, but only for cases about administrative acts done using that authority. The part of the precedent that conflicts with this will no longer be followed.
raw.held: A lawfully established body that the government has given public authority for specific matters can be a defendant in administrative lawsuits, limited to cases about administrative acts it takes using that authority. The 1971 Administrative Court precedent (No. 232) is no longer to be applied to the extent it conflicts with this.

points.text: People who think a central or local government agency's administrative act is unlawful or improper and harms their rights or interests may file appeals and administrative lawsuits.
So the defendant in an administrative dispute should in principle be the government agency that made the decision, and bodies outside government generally cannot be defendants.

However, a lawfully established body given public authority by a government agency for specific matters acts like a government agency within that authority, so it can be a defendant in cases about administrative acts using that authority.

The precedent said state-run enterprises set up under the Company Act are not government offices and so cannot be defendants; this broadly denied defendant capacity to all non-office bodies, which conflicts with the court's view, so that part is no longer applied.

Whether disputes under Article 84 of the Labor Standards Act belong in administrative or civil court is not covered by this ruling; if parties already got a final civil judgment, their right to sue was not harmed.

who: Bodies given public authority by government
Parties in Labor Standards Act Article 84 disputes

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Finance directive explaining what counts as a government 'affordable-price' public housing unit for a property tax cut was unconstitutional. The court decided the directive does not conflict with the Constitution. It reasoned that the directive stayed within the purpose and wording of the law.
raw.held: The 1975 Ministry of Finance directive explaining the meaning of this kind of public housing, for the half-rate house tax under Article 15, paragraph 2, item 1 of the House Tax Act, does not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: The Constitution requires paying taxes according to law, which covers both the scope of taxation and of exemption, and both must follow the written law. But when applying the law raises doubt, the responsible agency may interpret it in line with the legislature's purpose.

The half-rate house tax for government affordable-price public housing was meant to ease the burden on low-income people's homes, so it covers only housing sold at affordable prices to them, not homes the government sells otherwise.

The Ministry issued its directive to avoid doubt in applying the law, based on the legislative intent and the social and economic conditions of the time. It set conditions on size, buyer eligibility and price, and serves as a standard for finding the facts.
Because the directive did not go beyond what the law provides, it does not conflict with the Constitution.

The standard should be adjusted reasonably as conditions change, and the Ministry has since set other standards for particular cases, such as rebuilt housing for households whose illegal structures were demolished.

who: Low-income people buying government public housing
Ministry of Finance and tax authorities

raw.answer: The case asked whether a National Assembly delegate who has not taken the required oath may still carry out the duties of the office. The Court said no: a delegate who did not take the oath, or who deliberately did not take it in the legal form and with the legal wording, may not exercise the powers of the office. This adds to the Court's earlier Interpretation No. 199.
raw.held: The oath under Article 4 of the National Assembly Organization Act is an oath for exercising office. A delegate who did not take it, or who deliberately did not complete it in the legal form and wording, may not exercise powers. Interpretation No. 199 is supplemented accordingly.

points.text: The Court accepted the request because the requesting body had doubts about Interpretation No. 199 and asked for a supplementary interpretation, as earlier interpretations allow.

The oath is meant to let the person publicly and solemnly declare their resolve to obey the Constitution and carry out their duties lawfully on behalf of the nation's people. Under Interpretation No. 199 it is an oath for exercising office.
The oath is a formal act in public law. Its wording is fixed by the Organization Act, and its procedure and manner follow Articles 3 to 7 of the Oath Act.

A delegate who did not take the oath breaches the duty to do so and may not exercise powers. Where clear evidence shows deliberate departure from the legal manner or wording, the formal act is not treated as done, which equals not swearing, so powers may not be exercised.
Whether a delegate who has not properly sworn may attend meetings is left to the National Assembly to decide itself, under the principle of self-regulation of the assembly.

who: Delegates who did not swear or who deliberately swore improperly

raw.answer: The case asked whether a 1962 rule implementing the Public Servants Insurance Act was unconstitutional for limiting to five years the time an insured person could keep their insurance service years on record. The court decided the rule added a time limit that the law itself did not contain, goes against the constitution's protection of people's rights, and should not be applied.
raw.held: Article 68 of the 1962 enforcement rules, which limited reserved insurance years to five years and treated later re-enrollment as new enrollment, does not match the Act, adds a limit the law lacks, and is not to be applied.

points.text: The Act's Article 21 said that a person who left a job and chose to reserve their insurance years instead of seeking a refund would have all their original years count when they resumed insurance.
The Act's Article 24 authorized the making of enforcement rules but did not authorize limiting the substantive right of insured people to reserve their insurance years.
The enforcement rule's five-year limit, with later re-enrollment treated as new enrollment, added a period restriction the law does not contain.
Adding that restriction goes against the constitution's protection of people's rights, so the rule should not be applied.

who: Public servants who left their jobs and reserved insurance years
Public servants who later re-enrolled in insurance
The examining authority that issued the rule

raw.answer: The Legislative Yuan passed a resolution asking the Executive Yuan to pay civil servants and teachers an extra half month of year-end bonus this year, with the budget to be added later. The court decided this was a proposal to increase spending on a budget the Executive Yuan had submitted, which Article 70 of the Constitution forbids. The resolution therefore has no effect.
raw.held: The Legislative Yuan's resolution asking for an extra half month of year-end bonus, with the budget added later, conflicts with Article 70 of the Constitution and has no effect.

points.text: The Constitution has the Executive Yuan propose the budget and the Legislative Yuan vote on it, which separates the power to propose from the power to decide.

This split lets the Executive Yuan take the nation's finances, economy and yearly policy needs into account when drafting the budget, while the Legislative Yuan, representing the people, checks it to keep spending reasonable and avoid waste.

To carry out this purpose, Article 70 bars the Legislative Yuan from proposing increases in spending on the Executive Yuan's budget, in order to stop the government budget from growing and adding to people's burden.
The resolution asking for an extra half month of bonus, with the budget added later, was a proposal to increase spending on the budget.
It made no difference that the resolution was made as a proposal by members; in substance it still conflicts with the Constitution and so has no effect.

raw.answer: The case asked how school staff who were hired without passing a civil service exam should be treated under the Teachers and Educators Appointment Act. The court held that the rule requiring exam passage matches the Constitution, and that staff already hired before the act took effect do not gain the same appointment status as exam passers. They can only keep working at their current school, though the Examination Yuan may still test them to set their qualification.
raw.held: Article 21 of the act, requiring school staff to pass the relevant exams, is consistent with Constitution Article 85. The clause letting earlier-hired staff follow their old rules does not give non-passers equal qualification; they may only stay at their original school, and the Examination Yuan may still examine them to set their qualification.

points.text: Constitution Article 85 sets the principle that civil servants are chosen by open, competitive exams and may not be appointed without passing one.
Article 21 of the amended act requires school staff to pass the school administrative staff exam or an equivalent senior or ordinary civil service exam, which fits that principle.

The 1985 version required existing staff to take an exam set by the Examination Yuan, and let those who did not pass stay in their posts until leaving, balancing the exam principle with those staff's existing interests.

The 1990 amendment lets staff hired before the act follow their old rules as an exception, but this does not give non-passers the same qualification as exam passers, so they can only stay at their original school.
Since these staff lack a legally required exam qualification, the Examination Yuan may still hold exams for those willing to take them, to set their qualification.

who: School staff hired before the act without passing an exam
School staff who passed the required exams

raw.answer: The case asked whether Interior Ministry directives letting road authorities abolish non-planned roads (roads not in an urban plan) are unconstitutional. The court decided they are not, because within areas with a legally adopted urban plan, roads follow that plan. Once planned roads are built and open to the public, authorities may abolish a non-planned road that is no longer needed for public passage.
raw.held: Where an urban plan and its detailed plan have been legally adopted, roads must follow the plan. Once planned roads are open, the authority may abolish a non-planned road no longer needed by the public, and the two Interior Ministry directives on this do not conflict with the constitution's protection of people's rights.

points.text: Road planning in urban plan areas must follow the procedures in the Urban Planning Law, including a main plan and a detailed plan showing the road system.

Those plans are reviewed by a planning committee, put on public display where any citizen or group can comment, and then approved and published, so people have a chance to know about and comment on road arrangements.
Once the plan is fixed, it must be carried out, and drawing up the road system through this process already implies abolishing non-planned roads.

After planned roads are built and open, an authority may abolish a non-planned road with no continuing need for public passage, on its own initiative or on application, which fits the purpose of the Urban Planning Law.
The Interior Ministry's directives and Taipei's application rules match this view, so they do not conflict with the constitution's protection of people's rights.
The court added that abolishing existing alleys subject to public-use easement affects public interest, so clear rules in the urban planning regulations would be preferable.

who: Users of non-planned roads and alleys
Citizens and groups who comment on urban plans
Applicants seeking abolition or rerouting of non-planned alleys

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in the Act for Punishing Banditry, which sets death as the only penalty for kidnapping someone to demand ransom, violates the Constitution. The court decided it does not conflict with the Constitution. It reasoned that judges can still reduce the sentence in certain situations, so overly harsh punishment can be avoided.
raw.held: The death-only penalty for kidnapping for ransom in Article 2, paragraph 1, item 9 of the Act for Punishing Banditry is not unconstitutional, because sentence-reduction rules still apply.

points.text: The Act is a special criminal law that raises the penalty for kidnapping for ransom to deter this crime, protect public order and free people from fear of it.

The rule sets death as the penalty regardless of circumstances or results, which is very strict and could lead to unfair outcomes, so the legislature should review it with both people's rights and criminal policy in mind.
Article 8 of the same Act means the general part of the Criminal Code and Article 347, paragraph 5 still apply to these cases.
If the punishment is too heavy for the circumstances, a judge can reduce it under Article 59 of the Criminal Code.
If the victim is released without ransom being paid, the sentence may also be reduced under Article 347, paragraph 5.
Because these reductions can avoid overly harsh punishment, the rule is hard to call inconsistent with the Constitution.

who: People accused of kidnapping for ransom

raw.answer: The case asked whether rules requiring enforcement to stop against property that belongs to a bankruptcy estate are unconstitutional. The court decided they are not. It said the limit is needed so that all creditors can be paid fairly, and that the Judicial Yuan's guidance note only repeats what the law already says.
raw.held: Article 99 of the Bankruptcy Act, which limits creditors from enforcing against bankruptcy estate property, is allowed under Article 23 of the Constitution. The Judicial Yuan's 1982 enforcement guidance, item 9(1), adds no new limit on people's rights and does not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: Creditors have a right to ask the state to compel a debtor to pay, but it must be exercised by legal procedure and can be limited by law for reasons listed in Article 23 of the Constitution.
Under Article 99 of the Bankruptcy Act, bankruptcy claims can only be pursued through bankruptcy proceedings, so all creditors without a special priority right share the estate's property equally.

Starting or continuing court enforcement against estate property would hinder other creditors from being paid fairly, so it must be restricted. The restriction is necessary to prevent interference with others' rights and is permitted by Article 23.
The Enforcement Act says enforcement does not stop once begun unless the law provides otherwise, and the bankruptcy rule is such a legal exception.
Creditors with a pledge, mortgage or lien hold a special priority right and may exercise it outside bankruptcy proceedings, so the guidance excludes them from the stop.
The Judicial Yuan's guidance only points out the meaning of the Bankruptcy Act and Enforcement Act and adds no restriction or duty on people, so it does not conflict with the Constitution.

who: Creditors with priority rights over specific property

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Ministry of Finance's 1986 tax directive was unconstitutional in how it treated cases before and after it was issued. The court decided it was not. When an agency later changes its interpretation of a regulation, tax decisions already made and finalized under the earlier interpretation generally stay in place, unless the earlier interpretation was clearly unlawful.
raw.held: The Ministry of Finance's March 21, 1986 directive, which leaves finalized and already-paid cases unchanged and requires back taxes without penalty for cases not yet finalized or not yet paid, does not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: An agency's interpretation of a regulation explains the regulation's original meaning, is not an independent administrative order, and applies from the date the regulation took effect.

A later interpretation that differs from an earlier one does not make the earlier one automatically wrong. Decisions finalized under the earlier one are not affected, except where it was clearly unlawful, in order to keep the legal order stable.

Finalized court judgments can be revisited only through retrial when a legal ground for retrial exists. Decisions finalized without litigation may be changed by the agency only if the earlier interpretation was clearly unlawful and harmed people's rights.
The Ministry's directive fits these principles, so it does not conflict with the Constitution.

Under Article 28 of the Tax Collection Act, taxpayers may seek a refund within five years if the law was applied wrongly or the tax was miscalculated. This applies if the interpretation behind a tax decision was clearly unlawful.

If the law in force was applied correctly when the tax decision was made, a later change in the law or in the interpretation does not affect the finalized decision, and that refund rule does not apply.
The Ministry's 1980 directive was outside this interpretation, because it was not applied in the final judgment and the petitioner never sought administrative relief.

who: Taxpayers with unfinalized or unpaid tax cases
Tax authorities and the Ministry of Finance

raw.answer: The case asked whether a 1988 Ministry of the Interior rule was constitutional. The rule required people applying to register a superficies right (地上權) gained through long-term possession of someone else's land to show proof that their building was legal. The court held that, as applied to people who cannot produce such proof, the rule conflicts with the constitutional protection of property, so that part must stop being applied.
raw.held: The part of the Ministry's review guidelines requiring proof that a building is legal, when land is used for a building, is inconsistent with the constitutional protection of property and must stop being applied. If landowners and registered right holders dispute ground rent, the courts decide it.

points.text: The civil law rules on acquiring ownership or other property rights through long possession serve the public interest by pushing original owners to use their property responsibly and by respecting long-established situations, so property acquired this way is constitutionally protected.

The right to ask for registration of a superficies right gained by prescription is unrelated to whether the building on the land is legal; an illegal building is to be handled under building management rules.
Registering a superficies right and registering a building are two separate matters.
The Land Registration Rules, Article 70, concern registering legal buildings, but the Ministry's guidelines carried that requirement over to superficies registration.

As a result, possessors who proved they long, peacefully and continuously possessed private land intending to exercise a superficies right could not register it because they could not produce the legal-building proof, which conflicts with property protection.
Landowners keep their ownership but still bear taxes and similar burdens, so to balance both sides, by analogy to Civil Code Article 876, courts should decide rent disputes.

who: People who have long possessed private land and seek superficies registration

raw.answer: The case was about a Ministry of Civil Service directive from 1985 that stopped preferential-interest deposits on retirement pay for retired public employees who took new jobs paid from the public treasury. The court held that, for retirees who lump-sum retired and then work as contract-hired non-staff employees, the deposits should not be stopped across the board if the monthly interest cannot cover basic living needs. The directive was ordered to stop applying to the extent it conflicts with this.
raw.held: If the monthly interest on the preferential deposits of retirement pay and insurance old-age benefits cannot maintain a retiree's basic living (for example, if it is below the monthly salary of the lowest-grade, lowest-step appointed civil servant), the deposits must not be stopped across the board for such contract-hired non-staff workers. The part of the 1985 directive that conflicts with this must stop being applied.

points.text: The state should look after civil servants' livelihood by giving suitable retirement pensions, in line with the constitutional article on state organs handling retirement and old-age matters.
The preferential deposit scheme is a transitional measure, used until pay is raised generally or a pension system exists, to let retirees live on interest from their lump-sum retirement pay.
Barring retirees who take other publicly paid jobs from the deposits protects the retirement system and avoids double burden on the treasury, which is generally appropriate.
Retirees who take contract-hired non-staff jobs are mostly lower-level staff with small retirement pay, especially early retirees.

If their deposit interest falls below a basic-living level, such as the lowest appointed civil servant's monthly salary, basic livelihood is not secured, and their modest new earnings only supplement it, so deposits should not be stopped across the board.
These retirees differ from non-lower-level retirees and from those re-employed in publicly paid non-contract posts, so they cannot be treated the same.

who: Retired public servants and teachers who took a lump-sum pension
Retirees re-employed as contract-hired non-staff workers
